claim: In cancer cells, ATR signaling is crucial to tolerate the intrinsically high damage levels that normally block replication fork progression.
source: In cancer cells, ATR signaling is crucial to tolerate the intrinsically high damage levels that normally block replication fork progression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise for the study, drawing on established scientific understanding of cancer cell biology.

claim: Assembly of TopBP1 into condensates is required to amplify ATR kinase activity to the levels needed to coordinate the DNA damage response and manage DNA replication stress.
source: Assembly of TopBP1, a multifunctional scaffolding protein, into condensates is required to amplify ATR kinase activity to the levels needed to coordinate the DNA damage response and manage DNA replication stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous work (Frattini et al., 2021) and is presented as established knowledge from their research program.

claim: Many ATR inhibitors are tested for cancer treatment in clinical trials, but their overall effectiveness is often compromised by the emergence of resistance and toxicities.
source: Many ATR inhibitors are tested for cancer treatment in clinical trials, but their overall effectiveness is often compromised by the emergence of resistance and toxicities.
evidence: This statement references the current state of clinical research on ATR inhibitors, drawing on general knowledge of the field.

claim: AZD2858 disrupted TopBP1 assembly induced by the clinically relevant topoisomerase I inhibitor SN-38.
source: Among them, AZD2858 disrupted TopBP1 assembly induced by the clinically relevant topoisomerase I inhibitor SN-38, thereby inhibiting the ATR/Chk1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunofluorescence and western blot analyses.

claim: AZD2858 exerted its effects by disrupting TopBP1 self-interaction and binding to ATR in mammalian cells.
source: We found that AZD2858 exerted its effects by disrupting TopBP1 self-interaction and binding to ATR in mammalian cells, and by increasing its chromatin recruitment in cell-free Xenopus laevis egg extracts.
evidence: This is supported by TurboID proximity labeling experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: AZD2858 increased TopBP1 chromatin recruitment in cell-free Xenopus laevis egg extracts.
source: We found that AZD2858 exerted its effects by disrupting TopBP1 self-interaction and binding to ATR in mammalian cells, and by increasing its chromatin recruitment in cell-free Xenopus laevis egg extracts.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin extraction experiments from X. laevis egg extracts presented in the manuscript.

claim: AZD2858 prevented S-phase checkpoint induction by SN-38, leading to increased DNA damage and apoptosis in a colorectal cancer cell line.
source: Moreover, AZD2858 prevented S-phase checkpoint induction by SN-38, leading to increased DNA damage and apoptosis in a colorectal cancer cell line.
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis, PFGE, and apoptosis assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: AZD2858 showed a synergistic effect in combination with the FOLFIRI chemotherapy regimen in a spheroid model of colorectal cancer.
source: Lastly, AZD2858 showed a synergistic effect in combination with the FOLFIRI chemotherapy regimen in a spheroid model of colorectal cancer.
evidence: This is supported by synergy matrix analyses and spheroid viability assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: In every cell, thousands of DNA lesions are induced by endogenous and environmental agents.
source: In every cell, thousands of DNA lesions are induced by endogenous and environmental agents (Lindahl and Barnes, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lindahl and Barnes, 2000.

claim: Cells have evolved an intricate network of DNA damage response pathways that detect, signal, and repair DNA lesions.
source: To overcome their deleterious effects, cells have evolved an intricate network of DNA damage response pathways that detect, signal, and repair DNA lesions.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: DNA damage response pathways work in coordination with key physiological processes, such as cell cycle progression, chromatin remodeling, and transcription.
source: These pathways work in coordination with key physiological processes, such as cell cycle progression, chromatin remodeling, and transcription (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010; Jackson and Bartek, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciccia and Elledge, 2010 and Jackson and Bartek, 2009.

claim: Cancer cells typically exhibit higher levels of genotoxic stress than non-transformed cells due to their altered metabolism and high proliferation rate.
source: Cancer cells typically exhibit higher levels of genotoxic stress than non-transformed cells due to their altered metabolism and high proliferation rate (Jackson and Helleday, 2016; Luo et al., 2009; Macheret and Halazonetis, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Jackson and Helleday, 2016; Luo et al., 2009; Macheret and Halazonetis, 2015.

claim: Novel anticancer strategies aim to increase the sensitivity of cancer cells to genotoxic stress by targeting DNA damage signaling and DNA repair mechanisms.
source: As a complement to radiotherapy and chemotherapy that overload cancer cells with DNA lesions, the aim of novel anticancer strategies is to increase the sensitivity of cancer cells to genotoxic stress by targeting DNA damage signaling and DNA repair mechanisms (Jackson and Helleday, 2016; Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jackson and Helleday, 2016 and Brown et al., 2017.

claim: ATR signaling activates cell cycle checkpoints.
source: For example, ATR signaling activates cell cycle checkpoints (Brown and Baltimore, 2000; Eykelenboom et al., 2013; de Klein et al., 2000), promotes DNA repair (Tercero and Diffley, 2001), regulates the firing of replication origins (Toledo et al., 2013), and the cellular pool of deoxyribonucleotides (D'Angiolella et al., 2012; Le et al., 2017; Lopez-Contreras et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown and Baltimore, 2000; Eykelenboom et al., 2013; de Klein et al., 2000.

claim: ATR signaling promotes DNA repair.
source: For example, ATR signaling activates cell cycle checkpoints (Brown and Baltimore, 2000; Eykelenboom et al., 2013; de Klein et al., 2000), promotes DNA repair (Tercero and Diffley, 2001), regulates the firing of replication origins (Toledo et al., 2013), and the cellular pool of deoxyribonucleotides (D'Angiolella et al., 2012; Le et al., 2017; Lopez-Contreras et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tercero and Diffley, 2001.

claim: ATR signaling regulates the firing of replication origins.
source: For example, ATR signaling activates cell cycle checkpoints (Brown and Baltimore, 2000; Eykelenboom et al., 2013; de Klein et al., 2000), promotes DNA repair (Tercero and Diffley, 2001), regulates the firing of replication origins (Toledo et al., 2013), and the cellular pool of deoxyribonucleotides (D'Angiolella et al., 2012; Le et al., 2017; Lopez-Contreras et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Toledo et al., 2013.

claim: ATR signaling regulates the cellular pool of deoxyribonucleotides.
source: For example, ATR signaling activates cell cycle checkpoints (Brown and Baltimore, 2000; Eykelenboom et al., 2013; de Klein et al., 2000), promotes DNA repair (Tercero and Diffley, 2001), regulates the firing of replication origins (Toledo et al., 2013), and the cellular pool of deoxyribonucleotides (D'Angiolella et al., 2012; Le et al., 2017; Lopez-Contreras et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Angiolella et al., 2012; Le et al., 2017; Lopez-Contreras et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: The ATR signaling pathway is essential for the proliferation of cancer cells that display intrinsically higher levels of genotoxic stress.
source: The ATR signaling pathway is also essential for the proliferation of cancer cells that display intrinsically higher levels of genotoxic stress.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field of cancer biology.

claim: Several clinical trials are evaluating the efficacy of ATR inhibitors in patients with cancer.
source: Therefore, several clinical trials are evaluating the efficacy of ATR inhibitors in patients with cancer (Lecona and Fernandez-Capetillo, 2018), particularly cancers in which the oncogene CDC25A is overexpressed (Ruiz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lecona and Fernandez-Capetillo, 2018 and Ruiz et al., 2016.

claim: Kinase inhibitors often exert a strong selective pressure for the acquisition of drug resistance through kinase mutations.
source: However, as kinase inhibitors often exert a strong selective pressure for the acquisition of drug resistance through kinase mutations, alternative therapeutic options must be identified (Bhullar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bhullar et al., 2018.

claim: Targeting biomolecular condensates may provide conceptually novel approaches to drug discovery.
source: Unlike classical approaches that target the activity of a specific protein with small molecule inhibitors, recent cell biology advances suggest that targeting biomolecular condensates may provide conceptually novel approaches to drug discovery (Mitrea et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mitrea et al., 2022.

claim: Biomolecular condensates are subcellular compartments that selectively concentrate hundreds of proteins and nucleic acids, without a surrounding membrane.
source: Biomolecular condensates are subcellular compartments that selectively concentrate hundreds of proteins and nucleic acids, without a surrounding membrane (Banani et al., 2017; Mittag and Pappu, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017 and Mittag and Pappu, 2022.

claim: Biomolecular condensates underlie the spatiotemporal organization of multiple biological processes.
source: These structures underlie the spatiotemporal organization of multiple biological processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about biomolecular condensates.

claim: The aberrant properties of condensates have been implicated in many diseases, including neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy, cancer, and viral infections.
source: Moreover, the aberrant properties of condensates have been implicated in many diseases, including neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy, cancer, and viral infections (Mitrea et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mitrea et al., 2022.

claim: Condensate formation is typically driven by multivalent scaffold proteins that function as central nodes in molecular networks.
source: Condensate formation is typically driven by multivalent scaffold proteins that function as central nodes in molecular networks (Banani et al., 2017; Mittag and Pappu, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017 and Mittag and Pappu, 2022.

claim: In humans, the main ATR activator in S-phase is Topoisomerase IIβ binding protein 1 (TopBP1).
source: In humans, the main ATR activator in S-phase is Topoisomerase IIβ binding protein 1 (TopBP1), a scaffold protein that includes nine BRCA1 carboxyl terminal (BRCT) protein-protein interaction motifs (Kumagai et al., 2006; Wardlaw et al., 2014) and an intrinsically disordered ATR activation domain located between BRCT6 and BRCT7-8 (Kumagai et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumagai et al., 2006 and Wardlaw et al., 2014.

claim: TopBP1 is a scaffold protein that includes nine BRCA1 carboxyl terminal (BRCT) protein-protein interaction motifs.
source: In humans, the main ATR activator in S-phase is Topoisomerase IIβ binding protein 1 (TopBP1), a scaffold protein that includes nine BRCA1 carboxyl terminal (BRCT) protein-protein interaction motifs (Kumagai et al., 2006; Wardlaw et al., 2014) and an intrinsically disordered ATR activation domain located between BRCT6 and BRCT7-8 (Kumagai et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumagai et al., 2006 and Wardlaw et al., 2014.

claim: TopBP1 has an intrinsically disordered ATR activation domain located between BRCT6 and BRCT7-8.
source: In humans, the main ATR activator in S-phase is Topoisomerase IIβ binding protein 1 (TopBP1), a scaffold protein that includes nine BRCA1 carboxyl terminal (BRCT) protein-protein interaction motifs (Kumagai et al., 2006; Wardlaw et al., 2014) and an intrinsically disordered ATR activation domain located between BRCT6 and BRCT7-8 (Kumagai et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumagai et al., 2006 and Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: TopBP1 activates the ATR signaling pathway via the formation of biomolecular condensates, which appear as nuclear foci by immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: Recent studies indicate that TopBP1 activates the ATR signaling pathway via the formation of biomolecular condensates, which appear as nuclear foci by immunofluorescence microscopy (Frattini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frattini et al., 2021.

claim: ATR activation is a multistep process.
source: The available evidence suggests that ATR activation is a multistep process (Koundrioukoff et al., 2013; Egger et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koundrioukoff et al., 2013 and Egger et al., 2024.

claim: TopBP1 is recruited to ATR-activating DNA structures by MRE11.
source: TopBP1 is recruited to ATR-activating DNA structures by MRE11 (Duursma et al., 2013) and binds to RPA (Acevedo et al., 2016), ATRIP (Mordes et al., 2008), and the 9-1-1 complex (Delacroix et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2007) to form a stable ATR-activating complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duursma et al., 2013.

claim: TopBP1 binds to RPA, ATRIP, and the 9-1-1 complex to form a stable ATR-activating complex.
source: TopBP1 is recruited to ATR-activating DNA structures by MRE11 (Duursma et al., 2013) and binds to RPA (Acevedo et al., 2016), ATRIP (Mordes et al., 2008), and the 9-1-1 complex (Delacroix et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2007) to form a stable ATR-activating complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Acevedo et al., 2016, Mordes et al., 2008, Delacroix et al., 2007, and Lee et al., 2007.

claim: TopBP1 is phosphorylated by the basal kinase activity of ATR, triggering the assembly of TopBP1 condensates.
source: Then, TopBP1 is phosphorylated by the basal kinase activity of ATR, triggering the assembly of TopBP1 condensates (Frattini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frattini et al., 2021.

claim: TopBP1 condensation functions as a molecular switch that amplifies ATR activity up to the level required for signal transduction by the checkpoint effector kinase Chk1.
source: We found that TopBP1 condensation functions as a molecular switch that amplifies ATR activity up to the level required for signal transduction by the checkpoint effector kinase Chk1 (Frattini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frattini et al., 2021, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: A significantly higher number of TopBP1 foci was observed in HCT116-SN50 cells compared to parental HCT116 cells.
source: We first examined the number of TopBP1 condensates in the CRC cell lines HCT116 and HCT116-SN50 (50-fold more resistant to SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, than the parental HCT116 cell line) (Candeil et al., 2004) and observed a significantly higher number of TopBP1 foci in HCT116-SN50 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: HCT116-SN50 cells are 50-fold more resistant to SN-38 than the parental HCT116 cell line.
source: We first examined the number of TopBP1 condensates in the CRC cell lines HCT116 and HCT116-SN50 (50-fold more resistant to SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, than the parental HCT116 cell line) (Candeil et al., 2004) and observed a significantly higher number of TopBP1 foci in HCT116-SN50 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Candeil et al., 2004.

claim: Cry2 forms tetramers when exposed to 488 nm light and thereby nucleates the assembly of TopBP1 condensates.
source: Cry2 forms tetramers when exposed to 488 nm light and thereby nucleates the assembly of TopBP1 condensates (Frattini et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frattini et al., 2021.

claim: More than 300 molecules were identified as potential TopBP1 condensation inhibitors among the 4730 compounds screened.
source: We identified >300 molecules that could be potential TopBP1 condensation inhibitors among the 4730 compounds.
evidence: This is based on the screening results presented in the manuscript.

claim: 131 compounds were selected based on the best z-scores for further evaluation.
source: Then, we selected 131 compounds (based on the best z-scores) and assessed their effect on the ATR pathway activation in HCT116 cells using two complementary approaches.
evidence: This describes the screening methodology used in the study.

claim: The 10 most effective drugs were MCB-613, OTSSP167, AZD2858, P005091, tubercidin, dactolisib, physalin F, PFK158, PF562271, and torkinib based on their ability to inhibit Chk1 phosphorylation.
source: This allowed us to select the 10 most effective drugs (MCB-613, OTSSP167, AZD2858, P005091, tubercidin, dactolisib, physalin F, PFK158, PF562271, torkinib) based on their ability to inhibit Chk1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on the screening results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The strongest synergistic interactions were observed between FOLFIRI and AZD2858.
source: We observed the strongest synergistic interactions between FOLFIRI and AZD2858 (a known GSK-3β inhibitor).
evidence: This is based on synergy matrix analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: AZD2858 was efficient already at 1 µM.
source: Consequently, we focused our study on AZD2858, which was efficient already at 1 µM (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Co-incubation with AZD2858 resulted in a significant reduction in the number of endogenous TopBP1 condensates per nucleus.
source: Co-incubation with AZD2858 resulted in a significant reduction in the number of endogenous TopBP1 condensates per nucleus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Co-incubation with AZD2858 led to a decrease in the number of 53BP1 foci.
source: Co-incubation with AZD2858 also led to a decrease in the number of 53BP1 foci (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 53BP1 forms biomolecular condensates.
source: 53BP1 forms biomolecular condensates (Kilic et al., 2019) and might interact with TopBP1 (Cescutti et al., 2010; Bigot et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kilic et al., 2019, Cescutti et al., 2010, and Bigot et al., 2019.

claim: 53BP1 might interact with TopBP1.
source: 53BP1 forms biomolecular condensates (Kilic et al., 2019) and might interact with TopBP1 (Cescutti et al., 2010; Bigot et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cescutti et al., 2010 and Bigot et al., 2019, and the use of 'might' indicates this is not definitively established.

claim: Co-incubation with AZD2858 did not modulate the number of PML nuclear bodies.
source: Conversely, co-incubation with AZD2858 did not modulate the number of PML nuclear bodies, which are membrane-less organelles unlike the Arsenic treatment, which is known to induce the formation of PML nuclear bodies (Jaffray et al., 2023; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Arsenic treatment is known to induce the formation of PML nuclear bodies.
source: Conversely, co-incubation with AZD2858 did not modulate the number of PML nuclear bodies, which are membrane-less organelles unlike the Arsenic treatment, which is known to induce the formation of PML nuclear bodies (Jaffray et al., 2023; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jaffray et al., 2023.

claim: SN-38-mediated ATR signaling induction was severely reduced by co-incubation with 100 nM AZD2858, as indicated by the decrease in Chk1 phosphorylated at S345 and RPA32 phosphorylated at S33.
source: Western blot analysis showed that SN-38-mediated ATR signaling induction was severely reduced by co-incubation with 100 nM AZD2858, as indicated by the decrease in Chk1 phosphorylated at S345 and RPA32 phosphorylated at S33 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Co-incubation of AZD2858 with SN-38 or FOLFIRI did not affect the ATM pathway, as indicated by the unchanged levels of ATM phosphorylated at S1981 and Chk2 phosphorylated at T68.
source: Co-incubation of AZD2858 with SN-38 or FOLFIRI did not affect the ATM pathway, as indicated by the unchanged levels of ATM phosphorylated at S1981 and Chk2 phosphorylated at T68 (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The level of γH2AX was not affected by co-incubation with AZD2858 and SN-38 (or FOLFIRI) compared with SN-38 (or FOLFIRI) alone after 2 hours.
source: The level of γH2AX, a marker of DNA damage, was not affected by co-incubation with AZD2858 and SN-38 (or FOLFIRI) compared with SN-38 (or FOLFIRI) alone (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Similar results (decrease in Chk1 phosphorylated at S345 and unchanged γH2AX levels) were obtained after co-incubation with FOLFIRI+AZD2858 for 20 hr.
source: We obtained similar results (i.e. decrease in Chk1 phosphorylated at S345 and unchanged γH2AX levels) after co-incubation with FOLFIRI+AZD2858 for 20 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: AZD2858 significantly affects the ATR/Chk1 signaling pathway by inhibiting the assembly of TopBP1 condensates induced by the DNA-damaging agent SN-38.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that AZD2858 significantly affects the ATR/Chk1 signaling pathway by inhibiting the assembly of TopBP1 condensates induced by the DNA-damaging agent SN-38.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AZD2858 is a known glycogen synthase 3β (GSK-3β) inhibitor.
source: As AZD2858 is a known GSK-3β inhibitor, we asked whether its effects on the ATR/Chk1 signaling pathway might be mediated by inhibiting the GSK-3β pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AZD2858.

claim: SN-38-induced Chk1 phosphorylation at S345 was comparable in GSK3-β-depleted cells (shGSK3) and control cells (shLuc).
source: SN-38-induced Chk1 phosphorylation at S345 was comparable in GSK3-β-depleted cells (shGSK3) and control cells (shLuc) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The SN-38 and AZD2858 combination inhibited Chk1 phosphorylation in shGSK3 and shLuc cells, indicating that GSK-3β is not involved in Chk1 phosphorylation inhibition by AZD2858.
source: Moreover, the SN-38 and AZD2858 combination inhibited Chk1 phosphorylation in shGSK3 and shLuc cells, indicating that GSK-3β is not involved in Chk1 phosphorylation inhibition by AZD2858.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The combination of SN-38 and AZD2858 did not increase significantly the level of GSK-3β phosphorylated at S9, unlike what was observed with insulin.
source: The combination did not increase significantly the level of GSK-3β phosphorylated at S9, a marker of kinase inhibition, unlike what was observed with insulin, a well-known regulator of GSK-3β activity (Cross et al., 1995; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Insulin is a well-known regulator of GSK-3β activity.
source: The combination did not increase significantly the level of GSK-3β phosphorylated at S9, a marker of kinase inhibition, unlike what was observed with insulin, a well-known regulator of GSK-3β activity (Cross et al., 1995; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cross et al., 1995.

claim: Other more effective and specific GSK-3β inhibitors, compared with AZD2858, did not show any effect on light-induced optoTopBP1 condensation.
source: In addition, among the molecules tested from the TargetMol library, other more effective and specific GSK-3β inhibitors, compared with AZD2858, did not show any effect on light-induced optoTopBP1 condensation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Although AZD2858 is a GSK-3β inhibitor, its modulation of the ATR/Chk1 pathway is not due to this function.
source: These findings suggest that although AZD2858 is a GSK-3β inhibitor, its modulation of the ATR/Chk1 pathway is not due to this function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AZD2858 disrupts TopBP1 self-association and its interaction with its primary activator ATR.
source: Isolation of biotinylated proteins using streptavidin-coated beads highlighted a drastic reduction in TopBP1 proximity with recombinant and endogenous TopBP1 and also with ATR upon incubation with AZD2858 alone or with SN-38 (Figure 2D). These findings suggest that AZD2858 disrupts TopBP1 self-association and its interaction with its primary activator ATR.
evidence: This is supported by TurboID proximity labeling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Combining CPT and AZD2858 earlier enhances the accumulation of replication-related factors (RPA, TopBP1, and Pol ε) on chromatin compared to CPT treatment alone, particularly visible at 60 min after starting replication.
source: Our data demonstrate that combining CPT and AZD2858 earlier enhances the accumulation of replication-related factors (RPA, TopBP1, and Pol ε) on chromatin compared to CPT treatment alone, particularly visible at the 60 min after starting replication (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin extraction data from X. laevis egg extracts shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The enhanced accumulation of replication-related factors on chromatin may be due to increased origin activation, as normally seen when the S-phase checkpoint is inhibited.
source: This may be due to increased origin activation, as normally seen when the S-phase checkpoint is inhibited (Marheineke and Hyrien, 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Marheineke and Hyrien, 2004.

claim: AZD2858 acts primarily on the ATR signaling pathway through TopBP1 self-association inhibition.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that AZD2858 acts primarily on the ATR signaling pathway through TopBP1 self-association inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chk1 plays a pivotal role as a mediator of the S-phase checkpoint.
source: Chk1 plays a pivotal role as a mediator of the S-phase checkpoint (Stracker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stracker et al., 2009.

claim: BrdU incorporation was markedly reduced in SN-38-treated HCT116 cells, suggesting a slowdown of the S-phase.
source: BrdU incorporation was markedly reduced in SN-38-treated HCT116 cells, suggesting a slowdown of the S-phase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When SN-38 was combined with AZD2858, the effect on BrdU incorporation was partially reduced.
source: However, when SN-38 was combined with AZD2858, this effect was partially reduced (red arrows in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CldU tracks were shorter in HCT116 cells incubated with SN-38 alone.
source: As expected, CldU tracks were shorter in HCT116 cells incubated with SN-38 alone, while addition of AZD2858 significantly reduced the negative impact of SN-38 on replication fork progression.
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Addition of AZD2858 significantly reduced the negative impact of SN-38 on replication fork progression.
source: As expected, CldU tracks were shorter in HCT116 cells incubated with SN-38 alone, while addition of AZD2858 significantly reduced the negative impact of SN-38 on replication fork progression.
evidence: This is supported by DNA fiber analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a tendency for the SN-38-induced S-phase checkpoint to be weakened after 6 and 12 hr of co-treatment with AZD2858 and SN-38.
source: Moreover, the impact of the combination treatment becomes more pronounced over time. Indeed, there was a tendency for the SN-38-induced S-phase checkpoint to be weakened after 6 and 12 hr of co-treatment with AZD2858 and SN-38 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The combination of AZD2858 and SN-38 affects replication fork progression and disrupts the cell cycle homeostasis, likely by inhibiting the ATR/Chk1 signaling pathway.
source: These results indicate that the combination of AZD2858 and SN-38 affects replication fork progression and disrupts the cell cycle homeostasis, likely by inhibiting the ATR/Chk1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the combination treatment at 12 hr, there was an increase in the proportion of cells transitioning into S-phase, which were initially in G1 (BrdU-negative) and progressed to a mid-S DNA content state.
source: In the combination treatment, at 12 hr, we observed an increase in the proportion of cells transitioning into S-phase, which were initially in G1 (BrdU-negative) and progressed to a mid-S DNA content state (between 2N and 4N) (green squares) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The combined treatment led to a progressive accumulation of BrdU-positive cells with 4N DNA content, corresponding to cells that completed S-phase and progressed into G2 phase.
source: Finally, the combined treatment led to a progressive accumulation of BrdU-positive cells with 4N DNA content, corresponding to cells that completed S-phase (BrdU-positive) and progressed into G2 phase (4N DNA content) (red squares) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The combination of SN-38 and AZD2858 attenuates the S-phase checkpoint, thereby activating a compensatory post-replicative cell cycle checkpoint that arrests the cell cycle before mitosis.
source: This suggests that the combination of SN-38 and AZD2858 attenuates the S-phase checkpoint, thereby activating a compensatory post-replicative cell cycle checkpoint that arrests the cell cycle before mitosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: DSBs remained elevated after the combined treatment of AZD2858 and SN-38.
source: DSBs remained elevated after the combined treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by PFGE data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: γH2AX and cleaved PARP1 levels increased at later time points of incubation with AZD2858 and SN-38.
source: Additionally, γH2AX and cleaved PARP1 levels increased at later time points of incubation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The AZD2858 and SN-38 combination disrupts TopBP1 assembly, most likely by inhibiting ATR kinase activity amplification, a critical process for inducing the S-phase checkpoint and regulating DNA damage repair.
source: Altogether, these findings indicate that the AZD2858 and SN-38 combination disrupts TopBP1 assembly, most likely by inhibiting ATR kinase activity amplification, a critical process for inducing the S-phase checkpoint and regulating DNA damage repair.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: After 48 hr incubation with sublethal doses of SN-38 and AZD2858, the sub-G1 cell population was increased by 40% compared with untreated cells, indicative of apoptotic cells.
